name: Islamic feminism
summary: Islamic feminism seeks equality and justice for women and men within an Islamic framework. It holds that patriarchal readings of the Qur'an and classical jurisprudence, not Islam itself, produced discriminatory family laws and practices, and it calls for reinterpretation (ijtihad), women's equal voice in defining Islam, and legal reform backed by constitutions and human-rights standards.
scope: The faith-based reformist strand as defined by Margot Badran (Al-Ahram Weekly 2002, Countercurrents 2006): a feminist discourse and practice that derives its mandate from the Qur'an and seeks gender equality in the state, civil institutions and everyday life, with the Qur'an and ijtihad as its core; her named thinkers include Amina Wadud, Asma Barlas, Riffat Hassan, Ziba Mir-Hosseini and Aziza al-Hibri. The Musawah Framework (Mir-Hosseini and Zainah Anwar are on its planning committee) is read as its own programme statement on family law. It excludes secular Muslim feminists who reject the label and Islamist women's movements. The movement is about gender, family law and religious authority, so economic, foreign-policy and most constitutional statements are null.
